Invent a new x-ray detector technology f.answer:
A proposed “gap-funnel phonon counter” would combine a suspended bismuth soft-x-ray absorber with a phononic-crystal membrane and four gap-graded Ti/Al superconducting sensors. An absorbed 0.1–2 keV photon produces athermal phonons that are confined by the membrane and funneled into progressively lower-gap regions, where they generate quasiparticles. Microwave resonators measure the quasiparticle populations before thermalization; summing the four signals determines photon energy, while their relative amplitudes correct for absorption position. After each event, voltage-controlled normal-metal traps rapidly remove quasiparticles, avoiding the millisecond thermal recovery of conventional TES microcalorimeters.

Because it counts athermal excitations rather than measuring a temperature rise, the detector could simultaneously offer high energy resolution and speed: a design target of 0.2 eV FWHM at 1 keV, microsecond recovery, greater than 90% quantum efficiency, and thousands of frequency-multiplexed pixels per readout line. This would improve on state-of-the-art soft-x-ray detectors by reducing thermal-fluctuation noise, pileup, cryogenic wiring, and the usual trade-off between absorber efficiency, spectral resolution, and count rate.

A proposed “electron-cascade graphene calorimeter” would use a nanolaminate of 2–3 nm tungsten absorber sheets interleaved with graphene. A soft x-ray absorbed in tungsten creates hot electrons that escape into the adjacent graphene before transferring energy to the lattice. The interconnected graphene layers form an ultralow-heat-capacity electron reservoir whose temperature is measured through the phase shift of a proximitized-graphene Josephson microwave resonator. After measurement, a gated tunnel contact rapidly drains the hot electrons for active reset.

Separating x-ray stopping power from calorimetric heat capacity could provide greater than 95% efficiency from 0.2–2 keV, approximately 0.3 eV FWHM resolution at 1 keV, sub-microsecond recovery, and thousands of frequency-multiplexed pixels per line. It would improve upon TES microcalorimeters by suppressing lattice thermal-fluctuation noise and eliminating the usual trade-off between thick absorbers, energy resolution, and count rate.

Rather than collecting the charges once, gates circulate every carrier through a calibrated voltage drop hundreds of times; each passage emits an identical Neganov–Trofimov–Luke phonon packet into a phononic waveguide. A separate fast phonon channel measures the prompt energy, while the exact carrier count corrects fluctuations in how the x-ray energy was divided between ionization and heat.
